title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XLII
paragraphs:
How deeply I could scorn this man,
If charity did not forbid it!
—SHAKESPEARE: _Henry VIII_.
Soon after returning from his honeymoon, Lydgate made a professional visit to Lowick Manor. A letter had asked him to arrange a time to call.

Mr. Casaubon had never questioned Lydgate about the nature of his illness. Even to Dorothea he had shown no anxiety about how much it might shorten either his work or his life. On this subject, as on every other, he recoiled from pity. The suspicion that people pitied some aspect of his circumstances which they had guessed or discovered against his wishes was bitter enough. The thought of inviting an expression of sympathy by openly admitting fear or sorrow was therefore unbearable. Every proud person knows something of this feeling. Perhaps only a sense of fellowship deep enough to make every attempt at isolation seem small and mean, rather than noble, can overcome it.

But something now occupied Mr. Casaubon's thoughts that made the question of his health and life haunt his silences even more insistently than his writing, still unripe in the autumn of his years. Certainly that work could be called his central ambition. Yet in some kinds of authorship the chief product is the painful sensitivity accumulated in the author's mind. One knows the river is there only by a few streaks of water amid a vast deposit of unpleasant mud. That was the case with Mr. Casaubon's exhausting intellectual labours. Their most distinctive result was not the “Key to All Mythologies.” It was his unhealthy awareness that others denied him a standing he had never demonstrably earned; his constant suspicion that their opinions of him were unfavourable; the sad absence of passion from his efforts to achieve something, and his passionate refusal to admit that he had achieved nothing.

So the intellectual ambition that seemed to others to have consumed and dried him up offered no protection against injury, least of all injury from Dorothea. And now he had begun imagining possibilities for the future that somehow embittered him more than anything he had considered before.

Certain facts were beyond his power to alter. There was Will Ladislaw's existence, his defiant determination to remain near Lowick, and his frivolous attitude towards the possessors of genuine, certified learning. There was Dorothea's nature, always finding some new form of eager activity, and concealing even beneath submission and silence passionate reasons which it was irritating to contemplate. There were the opinions and sympathies that had taken hold of her on subjects he could not possibly discuss with her. He could not deny that Dorothea was as virtuous and lovely a young wife as he could have found. But a young wife proved more troublesome than he had imagined. She nursed him, read to him, anticipated his needs and worried about his feelings. Nevertheless, he had become certain that she judged him. Her wifely devotion seemed an act of penance for disbelieving thoughts. Along with it came a capacity for comparison that placed him and his work in an all too revealing light among things in general. Like vapour, his discontent passed through every gentle expression of her love and clung to the unappreciative world which she had merely brought closer to him.

Poor Mr. Casaubon! His suffering was harder to bear because it felt like betrayal. The young creature who had worshipped him with complete confidence had soon become a critical wife. Her early criticisms and expressions of resentment had left an impression no later tenderness or obedience could erase. His suspicious mind now read her silence as rebellion held in check. An unexpected remark asserted her awareness of her own superiority. Her gentle answers were irritatingly cautious; when she agreed, she was congratulating herself on her patience. The harder he struggled to hide this inner drama, the more vividly he experienced it, just as we hear more acutely a sound we hope nobody else will hear.

Far from finding Mr. Casaubon's resulting misery surprising, I think it quite ordinary. Cannot a tiny speck held close to our eyes blot out the world's splendour, leaving only a rim of light by which to see the obstruction? I know no speck more troublesome than the self. And if Mr. Casaubon had chosen to explain his grievances—his suspicion that he was no longer adored without criticism—who could have denied that he had good grounds? Indeed, there was a powerful reason to add which he had not explicitly considered: he was not entirely adorable. He suspected this, however, as he suspected other things without admitting them. Like the rest of us, he felt how comforting it would be to have a companion who would never discover the fact.

This painful sensitivity towards Dorothea was fully established before Will Ladislaw returned to Lowick. Events since then had driven Mr. Casaubon's talent for suspicious interpretation into furious activity. To the facts he knew, he added imaginary facts about the present and future. These became more real to him than the actual ones, because they aroused stronger dislike and a more overwhelming bitterness. Suspicion and jealousy kept weaving their web around Will Ladislaw's intentions and Dorothea's impressions. It would be quite unfair to suppose that he could have put any vulgar interpretation on Dorothea's conduct. His own habits of thought and behaviour, as much as the obvious nobility of her nature, protected him from that mistake. What he jealously guarded was her opinion: the influence that might guide her passionate judgments, and the future possibilities towards which they might lead her. Until Will's last defiant letter, he had had no definite charge he would choose to bring formally against him. Still, he felt justified in believing Will capable of any scheme that might appeal to a rebellious nature and uncontrolled impulses. He was certain Dorothea had caused Will's return from Rome and his decision to settle nearby. He was perceptive enough to imagine that she had innocently encouraged it. Clearly she was ready to become attached to Will and to yield to his suggestions. They had never talked alone without her coming away with some new, troublesome idea. The last such meeting that Mr. Casaubon knew about had led to a scene that made him angrier with them both than ever before. On returning from Freshitt Hall, Dorothea had for the first time said nothing about seeing Will. Her flood of ideas about money, poured out in the darkness of the night, had only introduced a mixture of still more hateful fears into her husband's mind.

And the recent blow to his health was always painfully with him. Certainly he felt much better. His usual capacity for work had returned. Perhaps the illness had been only exhaustion, and twenty years of achievement still lay ahead to justify thirty years of preparation. That prospect was sweetened by a taste of revenge upon the premature sneers of Carp and company. Even as Mr. Casaubon carried his little candle among the tombs of the past, those modern figures crossed its dim light and interrupted his patient exploration. To prove Carp wrong, forcing him to swallow his words with considerable indigestion, would be a pleasant incidental reward of literary triumph. The prospect of surviving through future ages on earth and for all eternity in heaven did not prevent him from dwelling on it. Since the expectation of his own endless bliss could not remove the bitter flavours of jealousy and revenge, it is less surprising that the likelihood of other people's brief earthly happiness after he had entered glory did little to sweeten his temper. If a disease really was undermining him, some people might have considerable opportunity to be happier once he was gone. If one of those people were Will Ladislaw, Mr. Casaubon objected so strongly that his resentment seemed likely to accompany him into a disembodied existence.

This states the case very baldly, and therefore very incompletely. The human soul runs in many channels. As we know, Mr. Casaubon had a sense of right and an honourable pride in fulfilling the demands of honour. These obliged him to find motives for his conduct other than jealousy and revenge. He put the case to himself like this: “When I married Dorothea Brooke, I undertook to provide for her welfare after my death. But ample property held independently does not guarantee welfare. On the contrary, circumstances could make such possessions a danger to her. Any man skilful enough to exploit either her passionate affections or her quixotic enthusiasm would find her easy prey. And there is a man here who intends exactly that—a man governed only by passing whims, and personally hostile to me. Of that I am certain. His hostility feeds on his awareness of his own ingratitude, and he has repeatedly expressed it by ridiculing me. I am as sure of this as if I had heard him. Even if I live, I shall worry about what he may try to accomplish by indirect influence. He has won Dorothea's ear and fascinated her. He has plainly tried to persuade her that he has claims on me beyond anything I have done for him. If I die—and he is staying here to watch for that—he will persuade her to marry him. It would be a disaster for her and a triumph for him. _She_ would not see the disaster. He could make her believe anything. She is inclined to excessive attachment, and secretly blames me for failing to respond to it. Already she is preoccupied with his fortunes. He imagines an easy conquest, and taking over my nest. I will prevent that! Such a marriage would ruin Dorothea. Has he ever persevered in anything except out of opposition? In learning he has always wanted an impressive show for little effort. In religion, he could easily echo Dorothea's peculiar ideas for as long as it suited him. When has shallow learning ever been separate from loose principles? I distrust his morals completely. It is my duty to do everything I can to prevent his plans succeeding.”

The arrangements Mr. Casaubon had made at his marriage left him free to take strong measures. But considering those measures inevitably made him dwell on his own chances of survival. At last his desire for the most accurate possible estimate overcame his proud reserve. He resolved to ask Lydgate what his illness was.

He told Dorothea that Lydgate had an appointment to visit at half past three. When she anxiously asked whether he had felt ill, he answered, “No. I merely wish to consult him about some recurring symptoms. You need not see him, my dear. I shall arrange for him to join me in the Yew-tree Walk, where I shall be taking my customary exercise.”

Entering the Yew-tree Walk, Lydgate saw Mr. Casaubon moving slowly away, his head bowed and his hands, as usual, behind his back. The afternoon was beautiful. Leaves from the tall lime trees drifted silently across the sombre evergreens; light and shadow lay sleeping side by side. Nothing broke the silence except the cawing of rooks, a lullaby to an accustomed ear—or that last, solemn lullaby, a funeral song. Lydgate, conscious of his own vigorous body in its prime, felt some pity as the figure he was about to overtake turned towards him. Coming closer, it displayed the signs of premature age more plainly than ever: a scholar's stooping shoulders, wasted limbs, and melancholy lines around the mouth. “Poor man,” he thought. “Some men of his age are like lions. You can tell nothing about their age except that they're fully grown.”
“Mr. Lydgate,” said Mr. Casaubon with his unfailing politeness, “I am most grateful for your punctuality. If you please, we shall talk as we walk up and down.”
“I hope you haven't asked me here because the unpleasant symptoms have returned,” said Lydgate, breaking a silence.

“Not directly—no. To explain my request, I must mention something that would otherwise need no reference. My life, insignificant in every other respect, may have some importance because the work that has occupied all its best years remains incomplete. In brief, I have long been engaged on a work I should wish to leave at least sufficiently advanced for publication by—others. If I knew that this was all I could reasonably hope for, such knowledge would usefully limit my efforts. It would guide me both in deciding what to undertake and what to set aside.”

Here Mr. Casaubon stopped. He brought one hand from behind his back and slipped it between the buttons of his single-breasted coat. To anyone with a deep understanding of human destiny, few things could have been more compelling than the inner conflict suggested by this formal, measured speech, delivered in his usual singsong, with the familiar movement of his head. Indeed, what could be more sublimely tragic than a soul struggling with the demand to abandon the work that has given its whole life meaning—a meaning destined to vanish like waters that come and go where nobody needs them? But nothing about Mr. Casaubon struck others as sublime. Lydgate, ready with a certain contempt for useless scholarship, felt a little amusement mingle with his pity. He knew too little of disaster yet to understand the pathos of a life in which everything fell below the level of tragedy except the sufferer's passionate self-concern.
“You mean the obstacles that poor health might put in your way?” he asked, trying to help Mr. Casaubon towards the point some hesitation seemed to be obstructing.

“I do. You have not suggested to me that the symptoms you observed with such painstaking care—which I must acknowledge—indicated a fatal illness. But if they did, Mr. Lydgate, I should wish to know the entire truth. I ask you to state your conclusions precisely, as a service of friendship. If you can tell me that nothing threatens my life beyond its ordinary accidents, I shall rejoice, for the reasons I have given. If you cannot, then knowing the truth matters still more to me.”

“Then I need no longer hesitate about what to do,” said Lydgate. “But first I must make you understand that my conclusions are uncertain for two reasons. I can make mistakes, and heart disease is particularly difficult to predict. In any event, it is scarcely possible to add much to life's already enormous uncertainty.”
Mr. Casaubon visibly flinched, but bowed.

“I believe you have what is called fatty degeneration of the heart. Laennec, who gave us the stethoscope not many years ago, first recognised and investigated the disease. We still need much more experience and longer observation of it. But after what you have said, I have a duty to tell you that it often causes sudden death. At the same time, that outcome cannot be predicted. Your condition might allow you another fifteen years of reasonably comfortable life, or even longer. Anything more I could tell you would consist of anatomical or medical details, leaving your expectations exactly where they are.” Lydgate was perceptive enough to know that Mr. Casaubon would take plain speech, without a show of excessive caution, as a mark of respect.
“Thank you, Mr. Lydgate,” said Mr. Casaubon after a brief pause. “There is one more question. Have you told Mrs. Casaubon what you have just told me?”

“In part—that is, about the possible outcomes.” Lydgate was about to explain why he had spoken to Dorothea, but Mr. Casaubon gave a slight wave of his hand, unmistakably wishing to end the conversation. He repeated, “Thank you,” and began commenting on the day's exceptional beauty.

Lydgate, sure that his patient wanted solitude, soon left. The dark figure continued pacing, hands behind his back and head bowed. The sombre yews offered silent companionship to his melancholy. Little shadows of birds or leaves flitted across the islands of sunlight, moving soundlessly as though in the presence of grief. Here was a man looking into death's eyes for the first time. He was passing through one of those rare moments when we feel the truth of a commonplace. That differs from what we call knowing it as much as the sight of water on the earth differs from the feverish vision of water that cannot be reached to cool a burning tongue. When “We must all die” suddenly becomes the sharp awareness “I must die—and soon,” death seizes us, and his fingers are cruel. Later he may gather us into his arms as our mother did, and our last dim moment of earthly awareness may resemble our first. Mr. Casaubon now felt as if he had suddenly arrived at the bank of the dark river and heard the splash of an approaching oar. He could distinguish no figures, but waited to be summoned. At such a time the mind does not abandon its lifelong inclination. Imagination carries that inclination beyond death and looks back, perhaps with the divine calm of generosity, perhaps with the petty anxieties of self-assertion. Mr. Casaubon's actions will give us a clue to his inclination. With certain private scholarly reservations, he considered himself a believing Christian, both in his judgments of the present and his hopes for the future. Yet what we seek to satisfy, even when we call it a distant hope, is a present desire. The future estate for which men toil in city alleys already exists in their love and imagination. Mr. Casaubon's present longing was not for divine fellowship and light free of earthly conditions. Poor man, his passionate desires clung close to the ground like mist in deeply shaded places.

Dorothea knew when Lydgate rode away. She stepped into the garden, her first impulse to go straight to her husband. But she hesitated, afraid of offending him by intruding. Her warmth, repeatedly rebuffed, combined with her intense memory to deepen her fear, as frustrated energy sinks into a shudder. She wandered slowly around the nearest groups of trees until she saw him coming. Then she moved towards him. She might have been an angel sent from heaven to promise that the few hours left would still be filled with faithful love—a love that held more closely now it understood his grief. His answering glance was so cold that her timidity increased. Even so, she turned beside him and slipped her hand through his arm.
Mr. Casaubon left his hands behind his back, letting her supple arm cling awkwardly to his stiff one.

The feeling this hard, unresponsive arm gave Dorothea was horrible. That is a strong word, but not too strong. Through acts we call trivial, the seeds of joy are continually squandered. Finally men and women look with haggard faces at the devastation their own waste has created and declare that the earth yields no sweetness, calling their denial knowledge. You may ask how Mr. Casaubon could behave like this and call himself a man. Remember that his mind recoiled from pity. Have you ever watched what happens to such a mind when it suspects that its own grief may bring satisfaction, now or later, to the very person whose pity already offends it? Besides, he understood little of Dorothea's feelings. It had not occurred to him that on this occasion they could be as strong as his own feelings about Carp's criticisms.

Dorothea kept her arm where it was, but dared not speak. Mr. Casaubon did not tell her, “I want to be alone.” He simply walked towards the house in silence. As they entered through the glass door on the east side, she withdrew her arm and stayed behind on the matting to leave him entirely free. He went into the library and shut himself in with his sorrow.

She went upstairs to her sitting room. Through the open bow window came the afternoon's tranquil splendour over the avenue, where the lime trees cast long shadows. But Dorothea saw none of it. She flung herself into a chair, unaware that dazzling sunlight fell on her. If it caused discomfort, how could she distinguish it from her inward misery?
She was swept up in a rebellious anger stronger than any she had known since marrying. Words came instead of tears:
“What have I done—what am I—to deserve this treatment? He never understands what's in my mind. He never cares. What good is anything I do? He wishes he had never married me.”

Hearing her own voice, she stopped and grew still. Like someone exhausted and lost, she sat seeing in a single glance every path her youthful hopes had taken, paths she could never find again. In the same miserable light she saw clearly her own loneliness and her husband's. They walked so far apart that she was forced to look at him from a distance. Had he drawn her close, she would never have examined him, never asked, “Is he worth living for?” She would simply have felt him part of her own life. Now she said bitterly, “The fault is his, not mine.” The shock through her whole being had overthrown pity. Was she to blame for believing in him, believing him worthy? And what exactly was he? She was quite capable of judging him—she who trembled as she watched for his glances, who imprisoned her best self and visited it only in secret so that she might become small enough to please him. In a crisis like this, some women begin to hate.

The sun was low when Dorothea decided she would not go down again. She would send word to her husband that she felt unwell and preferred to stay upstairs. Never before had she deliberately let resentment rule her this way. But now she believed she could not face him without telling him the truth about her feelings, and she must wait until she could speak without interruption. Her message might puzzle and hurt him. It was good that he should be puzzled and hurt. Her anger told her, as anger so often does, that God was on her side. All heaven, even if crowded with spirits watching them, must take her part. She had decided to ring the bell when someone knocked at the door.
Mr. Casaubon had sent word that he would dine in the library. He was very busy and wished to spend the evening entirely alone.
“Then I won't have dinner, Tantripp.”
“Oh, madam, won't you let me bring you a little something?”
“No, I feel ill. Please make everything ready in my dressing room, but don't disturb me again.”

Dorothea sat almost without moving through her inward struggle as evening slowly became night. Yet the struggle kept changing, like that of a man who first moves to strike someone and ends by mastering the desire to strike. Committing a crime requires no more energy than a determined act of submission when the soul's noble habits regain their strength. The thought that had taken Dorothea out to meet her husband could not stay away for long. She was convinced he had been asking whether all his work might soon be stopped, and that the answer must have pierced his heart. That conviction rose beside her image of him like a dim, admonishing figure, sadly reproaching her anger. It cost her a litany of imagined sorrows and silent cries that she might become the mercy those sorrows needed. But at last she resolved to yield. When the house was quiet and she knew it was nearly his usual bedtime, she gently opened her door. She stood outside in the dark, waiting for him to come upstairs with his light. If he did not come soon, she thought, she would go down and risk another wound. She would never again expect anything else. Then she heard the library door open. Slowly the light rose up the stairs, the carpet muffling his footsteps. When he stood opposite her, she saw how much more drawn his face had become. He gave a little start at seeing her. Without speaking, she looked up at him imploringly.
“Dorothea!” he said, gently surprised. “Have you been waiting for me?”
“Yes. I didn't want to interrupt you.”
“Come, my dear. You're young; you needn't lengthen your life by staying awake.”

The quiet, sorrowful kindness of those words brought Dorothea something like the gratitude we might feel after narrowly avoiding an injury to a helpless, wounded creature. She placed her hand in her husband's, and together they walked along the wide corridor.
